I force myself to think only positive thoughts
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: This strategy is socially anxious/interpersonal in content and is hard to integrate with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by war-zone danger cues, hypervigilant threat monitoring, and trauma-memory reactivation. The other strategies and threat/memory items coherently reflect trauma-related safety management, but rehearsing conversations before any interaction targets a different problem domain that is not represented elsewhere in Triggers, Threat, or Memory. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should plausibly feed back into triggers/threat/memory; this item does not connect well to those active nodes.

vignette: Kaelin's eyes still scan a room with a practiced intensity, a habit forged in the war-torn streets where he spent two years as a relief worker. It was during his time in the conflict zone that Kaelin witnessed the event that now haunts him: a marketplace bombing that killed dozens of civilians, including children, and left countless others injured. He recalls the sound of kids crying, the scent of smoke and blood, and the feeling of utter chaos. The memories still feel more real to Kaelin than his day-to-day experiences as a jeweler in a quiet American town. Sometimes, without warning, a sound or smell can transport him back to that moment. He might be working on a piece, lost in concentration, when the wail of a child in the street outside sends his heart racing and his mind reeling. Other times, he'll feel the full weight of emotions – fear, helplessness, and grief – without any clear image or memory to anchor them. As Kaelin navigates his daily routine, he is constantly on guard against potential threats. His gaze darts around a room, taking in possible escape routes and noticing objects that could be used as weapons. Even when others reassure him of his safety, Kaelin can't shake the feeling that danger lurks around every corner. He prefers to sit with his back against a wall, where he can see everyone and everything. To cope with these feelings of hypervigilance, Kaelin has developed a few strategies. When anxiety starts to spiral, he reminds himself that things could have been worse – after all, he made it out alive when many others did not. He also tries to force positive thoughts into his mind, dwelling on the good he's done as a relief worker and the people he's helped. Despite these efforts, Kaelin can't escape the sense of unease that pervades his life. Simple interactions with others have become fraught: he hates being touched unexpectedly, which always seems to make him jump. Even in quiet moments, Kaelin finds himself checking his surroundings for signs of threat – a habit that has started to bleed into his work as a jeweler. Customers sometimes comment on the way Kaelin's hands move with a precision that borders on anxiety, as if he's perpetually poised to respond to some unseen danger. His business partner has noticed the change too, remarking on how Kaelin seems more withdrawn and preoccupied than before his time in the war zone. Kaelin knows things can't go on like this forever. He's started to withdraw from social events and gatherings, citing work commitments or exhaustion as excuses. What he really fears is losing control – of his emotions, of his surroundings, of himself. The memories still feel too real, the threat too imminent. And yet, Kaelin knows that if he doesn't face these demons head-on, they'll continue to haunt him. That's why he's finally seeking help, after months of struggling in silence. Kaelin wants to learn how to quiet his mind and calm his nerves, to rediscover the sense of purpose and fulfillment he once felt as a relief worker. More than anything, he longs to be free from the grip of these memories – to make peace with what happened, and find a way to live in the present without being forever bound to the past.
